function-definition.why: A function is a rule that gives each input exactly one output. That single restriction is what makes mathematics predictable: if you could put 3 in and get two different answers out, nothing downstream would be reliable. Everything from a spreadsheet formula to a trading model is a function.
traps: Repeated *outputs* are fine — several inputs may share an answer. Only a repeated input with different outputs breaks it.
The vertical line test works because a vertical line is a single input: if it hits the graph twice, that input has two outputs.

code.note: A mathematical function must return the same output for the same input. A function in code that reads a database or a random number is not one in this sense — that difference matters when you reason about what your code does.

function-notation.why: ~f(x)~ is a name for a machine and a slot to feed it. Once you have the name, you can talk about ~f(3)~, ~f(a+1)~ or ~f(x)~ itself without rewriting the rule each time. It is notation that buys you the ability to discuss functions in general.
traps: ~f(3)~ does not mean ~f~ times 3. The brackets are a slot, not multiplication.
In ~f(x+2)~, the whole of ~x+2~ goes in wherever ~x~ appeared — including inside powers.

domain-range.why: The domain is what you are allowed to put in; the range is what can come out. Only two things usually restrict a domain in algebra: dividing by zero, and taking an even root of a negative. Finding the domain is the habit that stops you confidently reporting an answer the function cannot produce.
traps: In context the domain is often narrower than the algebra allows: a model of ticket sales has no meaning at ~x = -4~ tickets, however happily the formula evaluates.

function-from-context.why: Real models are almost always a fixed part plus a rate times a variable. Reading which number is which — and what each means in the situation — is the skill that turns algebra into something useful. The intercept is the starting amount; the slope is the per-unit change.
traps: Answer the question that was asked: ~C(5)~ is a cost, while solving ~C(h) = 90~ gives hours. Mixing up which variable you are reporting is the usual lost mark.
